title: Software Engineering Is Becoming Plan and Review — Louis Knight-Webb, Vibe Kanban

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 97%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents (Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex) and how they transform software engineering into plan-and-review work. Vibe Kanban is a coding-assistant product and developer tool for managing parallel AI coding-agent workstreams. The discussion spans planning, coding, code review, QA, and shepherding changes through to deployment. The talk assumes familiarity with AI coding tools and software engineering workflows. This is a conference talk with live product demonstrations. Ten direct transcript evidence anchors support the classification across coding-agent workflows, product demos, and business analysis.

summary: Louis Knight-Webb, founder of Vibe Canvas and Vibe Kanban and London AI Tinkers organizer, examines how AI is transforming software engineering into plan-and-review work. Before GitHub Copilot, engineers spent most time writing code; now that share has shifted to planning and reviewing. He identifies two approaches: a plan-based approach (detailed upfront planning, spec frameworks, interrogating models with questions) that reduces review cycles, and a review-heavy approach (YOLO prompts with iterative corrections) that wastes time in back-and-forth. He strongly favors planning, noting that 5 minutes of planning saves 30 minutes of reviewing AI-generated code. He maps work types onto a matrix: front-end feature development resists upfront planning due to statefulness and edge cases, favoring in-the-loop work, while back-end features, refactoring, and migrations suit plan-heavy test-driven approaches. Agent execution times are growing from seconds (Copilot) to 30 seconds (early Cursor) to 5-10 minutes (Claude Code), with front-end QA as the next major frontier. Crossing the roughly 5-minute human attention threshold forces behavior change; engineers must parallelize multiple agent streams, which motivated Vibe Kanban. He coins 'focus maxing' — designing interfaces so agents run as long as possible before yielding back to humans, avoiding constant context-switching. Future coding interfaces should help write tasks, QA work, review code, and shepherd changes until deployment. He then announces live on stage, using Vibe Kanban itself to create the shutdown blog post, that he is shutting down the company. Despite 30,000 monthly active users and 25,000 GitHub stars, the business model was unsustainable: the company was neither selling to enterprise nor reselling tokens, and users spent $30 on subscription then $3,000 with Codex. The project continues non-commercially. In Q&A, he reflects positively, saying he wouldn't do anything differently, and identifies key lessons: work with great people, learn what hard work means, and hire someone skilled at enterprise sales.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and agenda
sections.summary: Speaker introduces himself as founder of Vibe Canvas and London AI Tinkers organizer, cites SWEeBench leaderboard credentials, and outlines agenda: why engineering is becoming plan and review, balancing approaches, agent time horizons, and shutting down his company.

sections.title: Why software engineering is shifting to plan and review
sections.summary: Before Copilot, engineers spent most time writing code. AI tools progressively shrunk code-writing from Copilot line completion to Cursor page completion to Claude Code. Displaced time moved to planning and reviewing rather than being returned as free time; AI is an accelerant giving roughly 20 minutes back per 30 minutes of coding.

sections.title: The two approaches: Plan-based vs. Review-heavy
sections.summary: Plan-based approach uses comprehensive plan docs, spec frameworks, and model interrogation to reduce review rounds. Review-heavy approach YOLOs prompts and iterates corrections. Planning is strongly preferred because switching back and forth with a half-delivering agent is very time-consuming.

sections.title: The matrix: Feature development vs. migrations and maintenance
sections.summary: Front-end feature development resists specification due to statefulness, interactions, animations, and styles, favoring in-the-loop work. Back-end features, refactoring, and migrations suit plan-heavy test-driven development. Distilled takeaway: 5 minutes of planning saves 30 minutes of reviewing AI-generated code.

sections.title: The impact of agent execution time
sections.summary: Agent run times are growing as tools evolve from returning code to running type checkers to running Playwright MCP tests. Copilot took seconds, Cursor 30 seconds, Claude Code 1-2 minutes last year and 5-10 minutes this year. Waiting longer for higher accuracy is worthwhile. Next frontier: AI QA-ing front-end work within 9 months.

sections.title: Managing the five-minute agent threshold
sections.summary: Five minutes is roughly the limit of sitting and waiting. Beyond that threshold, behavior must change fundamentally. Engineers cannot watch agent logs for 20 minutes; they need a different way of thinking about software development.

sections.title: Parallelization and workflow management (Vibe Kanban)
sections.summary: Terminal maxing runs multiple agents in parallel so one finished task is ready as another completes. Vibe Kanban was built for this: multiple workspaces for any coding agent, diff review, GitHub-style comments, preview and click-to-resize. Speaker calls for new interfaces embracing multi-stream management.

sections.title: Vision for future coding interfaces and 'focus maxing'
sections.summary: Speaker coins 'focus maxing' — designing interfaces so agents run as long as possible before yielding back to humans, avoiding constant context-switching that fries the brain. Future coding interfaces should help write tasks and plan, help QA work, help with code review (since companies won't ship fully Vibe-coded work without checking), and help shepherd changes until deployment by monitoring PRs and reacting to comments.

sections.title: Announcement: Shutting down Vibe Kanban
sections.summary: Speaker announces live on stage, using Vibe Kanban itself to create the shutdown blog post, that he is shutting down the company. Demo shows setup script in a Git work tree, dependency installation, Codex agent selection, live preview, and opening a pull request through Cloudflare CDN. Despite 30,000 MAU and 25,000 GitHub stars, the business model was unsustainable: not selling to enterprise, not reselling tokens. Users spent $30 on subscription then $3,000 with Codex. Project continues non-commercially. Market is mature and 'no fun playing for eighth place.'

sections.title: Q&A: Next steps and reflections on the startup journey
sections.summary: In Q&A, speaker says he'll take time off and start another company; co-founder joining a lab; most team found jobs at Agent Labs. Looking back, he feels positive — wouldn't do anything differently, it was the most interesting work at the cutting edge of agents, and increased his value as a human. Key lessons: work with great people, learn what hard work really means, and hire someone good at selling to enterprise.
